lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: By 1858, London had been using the River Thames as a toilet for decades. Nobody important seemed to mind.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: The same river, incidentally, supplied a lot of the city's drinking water.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Thousands of people were dying of cholera. Parliament decided the sensible thing to do was keep scheduling meetings about it.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: The summer of 1858 arrived, temperatures soared, and the Thames started producing a smell bad enough to get its own name. The Great Stink.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Parliament had recently moved into a beautiful new building. Unfortunately, they had also built it next to the Thames. With windows.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: They soaked the curtains in chemicals.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Then workers spread hundreds of tons of lime along the riverbanks. Which was essentially putting deodorant on a corpse.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: At one point, future Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli was seen leaving a committee room in a hurry, handkerchief pressed to his face.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: At the time, most doctors believed disease spread through foul air. So to the politicians breathing it every day, the smell now looked like a threat to them personally.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: A sewer plan that had been put off for years was approved in eighteen days.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: The Times summed it up quite nicely. Parliament had been forced to act by the force of sheer stench.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: The engineer, Joseph Bazalgette, built over a thousand miles of sewers, and made the pipes far wider than his maths said he needed. Just in case.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: London's population has more than tripled since. Those oversized pipes turned out to be a pretty good investment.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: And the part nobody saw coming? Cholera doesn't spread through bad air. It spreads through dirty water.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: So Parliament built the sewers to get rid of a smell, and ended up helping to protect London's drinking water. The city's last major cholera outbreak came in 1866. Subscribe for more.
